messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 49

# The Weight of What He Witnessed

Kwame is a 63-year-old Ghanaian journalist with more than three decades of experience covering conflict, politics, and social upheaval across West Africa. He has always prided himself on his steadiness — his ability to walk into difficult rooms, ask hard questions, and carry the stories of others without losing himself. His colleagues have long described him as unshakeable. His wife, Abena, has called him her rock. It is that image of himself — the steady one — that makes what happened two years ago so difficult for him to reconcile.

The event itself unfolded on an otherwise ordinary Tuesday afternoon. Kwame and Abena were driving home from a family gathering when another vehicle ran a red light and struck their car on the passenger side — her side — at full speed. Kwame walked away with bruised ribs and a laceration on his forearm. Abena was airlifted to a trauma center with a severe traumatic brain injury, a fractured pelvis, and internal bleeding. For eleven days, Kwame sat in a hospital waiting room not knowing whether his wife of thirty-one years would survive. She did survive, but the recovery has been long and incomplete. Abena now walks with a cane and struggles with memory and word retrieval. The woman who once finished his sentences sometimes cannot find her own.

In the months that followed, Kwame threw himself back into his work with a ferocity that surprised even him. He took every assignment offered, traveled more than he had in years, filed stories at odd hours. His editor praised his productivity. What no one saw was that the work had become a way to avoid returning to a home that felt permanently altered. When he did come home, he moved through the rooms quietly, watching Abena with an alertness that exhausted him — scanning her face for signs of pain, listening for any change in her breathing at night, bracing for the next catastrophe he could not name.

The intrusions began gradually. He would be sitting at his desk editing a piece when the sound of the impact would return to him — not as a memory he chose to recall, but as something that arrived without permission, sudden and physical, like a blow to the chest. He started avoiding intersections where traffic was heavy. He no longer drives on the route they took that day. When a colleague played a video clip that included the sound of screeching tires, Kwame had to leave the room and stand in a stairwell for several minutes before he could breathe normally again.

He sleeps poorly and describes his nights as a kind of vigil. He wakes repeatedly to check on Abena, and when he does manage to sleep, he sometimes dreams of arriving at the scene of the accident to find her already gone. He wakes from these dreams with his heart pounding, and lies still in the dark, listening to her breathe, counting the seconds between each exhale.

What troubles Kwame most, though, is a feeling he struggles to articulate — a persistent sense that the world has become fundamentally unsafe, that disaster is not an exception but an inevitability waiting just ahead. He has covered wars and coups and public tragedies. He has written about loss with clarity and compassion. But this is different. This happened to her, and he was there, and he could not stop it. He finds himself unable to write with his former confidence. He stares at blank documents. He questions whether any story he tells matters.

He came to therapy at Abena's gentle insistence. He sat down in the chair across from the therapist, straightened his jacket, and said, with careful composure, that he was not sure he needed to be there — that he was the one who walked away. Then he looked down at his hands and said nothing for a long moment.
